content.title: About
content.content: White icing is a sweet confectionery paste typically made from powdered sugar, egg whites, water, and a touch of lemon juice. It is used to coat cakes, cupcakes and cookies, giving them a smooth glossy finish and a delicate sweet flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The term “icing” comes from the English word meaning “coating” or “frost”.
White icing is a staple in traditional English and American cakes such as the “pound” cake and “fondant”.
To achieve a firmer texture the icing is sometimes heated to about 70 °C and then rapidly cooled.
Adding a small amount of cornstarch makes the icing more resistant to running.

items.title: Quick source of energy
items.content: The powdered sugar in the icing is rapidly absorbed, providing an immediate glucose boost.

items.title: Contains a small amount of vitamin C
items.content: Lemon juice, often added to the icing, supplies vitamin C, which supports the immune system.

items.title: Easily digestible
items.content: The low fat content makes icing lighter than butter‑based frostings.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can raise blood glucose levels and contribute to tooth decay.

items.title: Egg white allergy
items.content: Some individuals are allergic to egg whites, a common ingredient in icing.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice may irritate a sensitive stomach.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Icing is applied to cooled baked goods using a pastry bag, spatula or spoon. If needed, it can be thinned with water or thickened with more powdered sugar to adjust consistency.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store prepared icing in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 5 days. Before use, bring it to room temperature and give it a gentle stir if necessary.
